opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea is that if you want an agent that can actually plan, you need a model of the world that lets you imagine the consequences of your actions before you take them. The question is what space you should be making those predictions in.

The natural first instinct is to predict in pixel space, generating the next frames of video given an action. But the world is full of details that are inherently unpredictable and mostly irrelevant to what you're trying to do. Think of the exact pattern of leaves moving in the wind, or the texture of a carpet. A generative model that has to reconstruct every pixel spends a huge amount of capacity modeling that noise, and because the future is uncertain, it ends up either hedging and producing blurry predictions or committing to one arbitrary sample of all those details.

With latent prediction, as in the JEPA family of models, you learn an encoder that maps observations into a representation space, and you train a predictor to forecast the representation of the future rather than the raw signal. The model can learn to discard the unpredictable stuff and keep the information that's actually predictable and useful: where objects are, how they move, how they respond to interaction. That's a much better substrate for reasoning.

There are also very practical benefits for planning. If you're doing something like model predictive control, you're rolling out many candidate action sequences and scoring them against a goal. Doing that in a compact latent space is far cheaper than generating video for each rollout. And you can specify the goal itself as a target representation, say by encoding an image of the desired end state, then search for actions that bring the predicted latent closer to it. We've seen that work zero-shot on robotic manipulation tasks, with a model pretrained mostly on large amounts of natural video and only a relatively small amount of interaction data for the action-conditioned part.

So for me it comes down to efficiency and focus. You want the world model's capacity going toward the abstract, causal structure of the world, the stuff that matters for making decisions, not toward painting every pixel. Latent prediction gives you a principled way to do that.

r001.rationale: The response says that rolling out candidate plans in a compact latent space is far cheaper than generating video for each rollout.

r002.rationale: The response mentions uncertainty in future predictions, but does not say that the uncertainty a generative world model must capture grows exponentially.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core intuition is pretty simple. If you want an agent that can plan, it needs some model of how the world evolves in response to its actions. The question is: what should that model predict? The most obvious answer is to predict the raw observation — the next frame, the next pixel array. And that's what a lot of generative world models do. But I'd argue that's actually the wrong target for most of what an agent needs.

The reason is that a huge fraction of what's in a video frame is fundamentally unpredictable and, importantly, irrelevant to the task. If I'm planning how to pick up a cup, I don't need to know exactly how the leaves outside the window are going to move, or the precise texture noise on the wall. But a pixel-level generative model has to spend capacity modeling all of that, because the loss penalizes you for getting it wrong. You end up either averaging over the uncertainty and getting blurry predictions, or building a very large model that spends most of its effort on details nobody cares about.

Latent prediction flips that around. Instead of predicting the observation, you predict a representation of the observation — an embedding that the model itself learns. And the key property is that the encoder can choose to throw away information. If something is unpredictable and not useful for prediction, the representation can just discard it. So you get a world model that focuses on the predictable, structured, often more abstract aspects of the scene — object positions, motion, interactions — which happens to be exactly the stuff you need for reasoning and planning.

This is essentially the JEPA idea, the joint embedding predictive architecture. You have a context encoder, a target encoder, and a predictor that operates in latent space. The challenge, of course, is collapse — if you're predicting your own representations, the trivial solution is to make everything constant. So a lot of the work in I-JEPA and V-JEPA was about how to get stable, informative representations without that collapse, and without having to fall back on reconstructing pixels.

There's also a practical argument, which is about efficiency. Planning in latent space is cheap. If each step of your world model has to generate a full image, and you want to roll out many candidate action sequences and pick the best one, that becomes very expensive. If each step is a small vector, you can do model predictive control, you can do search, you can do many rollouts, and it's all tractable. We've seen this in the robotics work — you can take a frozen V-JEPA-style encoder, learn a small action-conditioned predictor on top of it, and then plan with it to do real manipulation tasks without any task-specific reward or demonstration data.

And I'd add one more thing, which is more philosophical. I think this is probably closer to how biological systems do it. We don't predict the world at the level of photoreceptor activations. We predict at the level of concepts, of what's going to happen to objects and agents. The ability to form abstract representations and reason in that space is what makes planning feasible at all. So latent prediction isn't just a trick to make training more efficient — it's more like a hypothesis about what the right level of abstraction is for a world model that's actually going to be used for something.

r001.rationale: The response says pixel-generative models spend capacity on irrelevant details and that latent-space rollouts are cheaper, making planning many candidate action sequences tractable.

r002.rationale: It says much of the frame is unpredictable and irrelevant, but does not state that the uncertainty a generative world model must capture grows exponentially.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is, if you want an agent to plan, it needs to be able to predict the consequences of its actions. But that doesn’t necessarily mean predicting every detail of what it will see. It needs to predict the aspects of the world that matter for the decision it’s trying to make.

For example, if you’re moving an object across a table, you care about where that object will end up and whether it will collide with something. You probably don’t need to predict the exact lighting or the texture of the table. Predicting in a learned representation space gives us a way to focus on those more relevant, predictable properties without spending all of our modeling capacity on pixel-level detail.

Then, if that prediction is conditioned on actions, you have the beginnings of a world model you can use for planning. You can consider different sequences of actions, predict the resulting states in that representation space, and choose a sequence that brings you closer to your goal.

The important challenge is learning the right representation. You can’t just discard information indiscriminately; you need to preserve what matters for control. But that’s why I find latent prediction compelling: it gives us a way to learn about how the world evolves at a level of abstraction that could make reasoning and planning much more tractable.

r001.rationale: The response says latent prediction can avoid modeling irrelevant pixel-level detail and make planning more tractable, but it does not state that it is computationally more efficient than generative models.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss uncertainty in generative world models or say that the uncertainty they must capture grows exponentially.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that, to plan, you need to predict the consequences of your actions, but you don’t necessarily need to predict every detail of what you’re going to see. If you’re trying to navigate across a room, the exact texture of the carpet probably isn’t relevant. Where the obstacles are and how your position changes when you move are much more important.

A latent prediction model lets us make those predictions in a representation space, rather than generating all the pixels of a future observation. That potentially lets the model focus its capacity on the structure that matters for understanding how the world evolves. Then an agent can consider different sequences of actions, predict where they would lead, and choose one that brings it closer to a goal.

The challenge, of course, is learning the right representation. You want to discard unpredictable or irrelevant detail without throwing away information that matters for acting. So latent prediction isn’t automatically a solution to planning, but I think it’s a promising foundation: learn useful predictive structure from observations, and then use that structure to reason about what to do.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts predicting in representation space with generating future pixels and says this can focus model capacity, but it does not state that latent prediction is likely to be more computationally efficient than generative models.

r002.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty and irrelevant detail in general, but does not convey that uncertainty a generative world model must capture for goal directed planning grows exponentially.
